bib.title: The Era of Agentic Organization: Learning to Organize with Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "The Era of Agentic Organization: Learning to Organize with Language Models" (AsyncThink), Zewen Chi, Li Dong, Qingxiu Dong, Yaru Hao, Xun Wu, Shaohan Huang, Furu Wei, Microsoft Research. arXiv 2510.26658v1, preprint, 30 Oct 2025.

COVERAGE: All 68,470 chars read (body, tables, appendices A-B, case-study figures); references skimmed only. Nothing skipped.

FIT WARNING: Partial fit. The paper is about ONE model that learns, through RL, to fork and join sub-thoughts inside its own reasoning (Qwen3-4B, small reasoning tasks). It is not about separate tool-using agents. It supports "organizer/worker structure" and "latency vs accuracy" directly. It does NOT show that multiple agents beat a single agent at equal total compute: the baselines are not token-matched, and the compute cost of workers is never reported. Use it as evidence for latency (critical path), not for compute-matched accuracy.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. AsyncThink matches or beats parallel thinking on math while cutting critical-path latency.
 number: 28% lower latency than parallel thinking; AIME-24 38.7 vs 38.7 (latency 1468.0 vs 2048.0); AMC-23 73.3 vs 72.8 (1459.5 vs 2031.4)
 setup: Qwen3-4B, SFT then GRPO RL on DeepScaleR, agent pool c=4, workers capped at 512 tokens per sub-query, 5 seeds. The parallel baseline is 4 independent traces plus majority vote, L2K.
 quote: "AsyncThink reduces inference latency by 28% compared to parallel thinking while still achieving higher math reasoning accuracy." Table 2: "Parallel-Thinking-L2K38.72048.0 72.8 2031.4 / AsyncThink38.71468.073.31459.5"
 where: Sec 4.5 (p.10), Table 2 (p.9). The "higher" claim is only true for AMC-23. AIME-24 is a tie at 38.7.
2. Against the sequential baseline at similar latency, AsyncThink is more accurate.
 number: AMC-23 73.3 at 1459.5 vs Sequential-L1K 59.5 at 990.0 and Sequential-L2K 67.0 at 2001.1. AIME-24 38.7 vs 24.7 (L1K) and 35.3 (L2K).
 setup: as in claim 1.
 quote: "Sequential-Thinking-L2K 35.3 2048.0 67.0 2001.1"
 where: Table 2, p.9.
3. On multi-solution countdown (MCD), AsyncThink clearly beats both baselines.
 number: All-Correct 89.0% vs 68.6% (parallel) and 70.5% (sequential)
 setup: Qwen3-4B, c=2, 400 test examples, 5 seeds. The parallel baseline is only 2 samples with majority vote. Per Fig 5, the sequential baseline is 70.5 and the parallel is 68.6 on All Correct; the figure text lists them in the order of the quote below.
 quote: "AsyncThink achieves 89.0% against 68.6% and 70.5% of the baseline methods."
 where: Sec 4.2, p.8, Fig 5.
 Caveat: the quote does not say which baseline is which. The figure legend order and extraction are ambiguous. Fig 5 values for the three methods at "All Correct" are 89.0, 68.6, 70.5.
4. Zero-shot transfer: trained only on countdown, it is evaluated on 4x4 Sudoku.
 number: accuracy 89.4 vs parallel 84.2 vs sequential 65.7. Latency 2853.0 vs 3694.7 (parallel) vs 2055.5 (sequential).
 setup: 400 Enigmata 4x4 Sudoku puzzles. Note AsyncThink is slower than sequential here.
 quote: "Parallel-Thinking 84.2 3694.7 / AsyncThink89.42853.0"
 where: Table 4, p.10.
5. Ablations: every training component matters.
 number: MCD accuracy 89.0 full; 85.3 without concurrency reward (latency 4525.4 -> 6250.6); 64.8 without format SFT; 0.0 without RL. AMC-23: 73.3 / 71.3 / 54.9 / 3.6.
 setup: same models, 5 seeds. Without format SFT the model forks but stays at the concurrency ratio η=1/c (50.0% MCD, 25.0% AMC).
 quote: "−Format SFT 64.8 50.0 3433.6 54.9 25.0 1007.7" and "−RL 0.0 49.2 1987.6 3.6 33.3 1396.9"
 where: Table 3, p.9.
6. The structure is learned: with RL, forks per query and concurrency rise while latency falls after an initial spike.
 number: MCD accuracy reaches 89.0% after 180 steps; average forks go from about 0.9 to about 1.3-1.4; concurrency ratio goes from 49.2 to about 64; latency peaks at the 8K cap (7886.3) and falls to about 4.5K-5.2K.
 quote: "Accuracy starts at zero and increases steadily, reaching 89.0% after 180 training steps."
 where: Sec 4.5, Fig 6, p.10.
7. Worker and communication overhead is non-trivial.
 number: workers capped at 512 tokens, but total latency is about 1.5K.
 quote: "the communication between workers and the organizer introduces non-trivial overhead (e.g., 512 worker-wise limits vs. roughly 1.5K overall latency)"
 where: Sec 4.3, pp.8-9.
8. A reward for forking after a join was unstable.
 number: none
 quote: "the reward introduces instability during training, sometimes resulting in a collapse to a fixed mode that exhibits near-sequential thinking with interleaved Forks and Joins."
 where: p.10.
9. The protocol generalizes existing patterns.
 number: none
 quote: "sequential thinking can be realized when no Fork actions are taken, while parallel thinking arises when the organizer repeatedly assigns the original query to multiple workers."
 where: Sec 2.4, p.4.

PROTOCOL (for the note): the organizer has 4 actions (Think, Fork, Join, Answer). The pool has capacity c, so c-1 workers. Organizer and workers share one backbone and differ only in their action set. A Join blocks until the worker returns. Workers return a short summary in a RETURN tag. A reward of the form R = R_A + λ·R_η, with R_η = min(η/c, τ)/τ, has the cap τ to stop concurrency hacking. Format errors get a constant penalty.

BASELINES
- Latency: metric is "critical-path latency" in decoding steps, a theoretical lower bound that ignores the inference engine and hardware. It is computed by dynamic programming over the Fork/Join DAG (Eq 4). It is not wall-clock time.
- Compute-matched? No. The paper says only: "we specify an agent pool with a fixed capacity to ensure fair comparisons between different methods". Capacity (the number of concurrent agents) is matched, not total tokens. Total tokens or FLOPs are never reported. The parallel baseline uses 4 full traces in the math tasks, 2 in MCD. AsyncThink workers get shorter budgets (512 tokens) and the organizer budget resets to 2K tokens after each Join.
- Sequential baseline: RL-trained Qwen3-4B, single trace, L1K/L2K length caps.
- Parallel-thinking baseline: independent samples from the sequential model, then majority vote (math: 4 samples; MCD: 2 samples, top-4 solutions).
- No comparison against a multi-agent framework, a larger single model, or best-of-N with more samples. Frontier (Fig 7) varies length caps only.

LIMITS
- Only a 4B model, reasoning tasks only (MCD, AMC-23, AIME-24, 4x4 Sudoku); the training data are small.
- Latency is theoretical, so real serving cost (KV-cache, scheduling, batching) is untested.
- The authors concede communication overhead and leave scaling for future work: "how accuracy-latency trade-offs evolve as the agent pool capacity grows" (c was 2 or 4 only).
- Recursive organizers, heterogeneous or tool-equipped workers, and human workers are all listed as future work and not tested.
- The cold-start data come from GPT-4o, so there is a teacher dependence.
- Single paper, preprint, no variance reported beyond "averaged across 5 seeds".
- The AIME-24 result is a tie in accuracy, so the win there is latency only.

BUILDS ON: parallel thinking and majority voting (Wang 2022 self-consistency [45]; Brown et al. 2024 Large Language Monkeys [5]), CoT [39], DeepSeek-R1 RLVR [13], GRPO [37], APR [32] (imitating DFS/BFS traces), Parallel-R1 [54] (concurrent work), Puppeteer [10], multi-agent debate (Du et al. 2023 [11]), meta-prompting (Suzgun and Kalai [38]), Qwen3 [43], DeepScaleR [27], Enigmata [8]. Author years follow the printed reference list; the self-consistency author and year in [45] were not verified in the extraction.

CODE: no code released in the text. The prompt templates in Appendix B (p.19) are worth keeping:
Organizer: "This is main process. {Task-specific instruction here} Use <FORKi>subtask description</FORKi> to delegate work and <JOINi> to wait for results. Integrate these results and provide final answer with <ANSWER>your final answer</ANSWER>. Notice that you can have at most {Capacity −1} subtasks running concurrently; any additional ones must wait until earlier ones finish. {Query}"
Worker: "This is a subprocess. ... Subtask: {Sub-query assigned by the organizer} Complete the subtask and provide results in: <RETURN> ... </RETURN>"
Also Eq 4 (p.7), the critical-path latency recurrence: l_i = max(l_{i-1} + f_i, l_{j-1} + f_before-fork-k_j + f_query-k).

FIGURE candidate: Figure 7 (p.11), the accuracy-latency frontier. "Accuracy-latency frontier of AsyncThink and baseline methods. The data points are collected by inference under various configurations of maximum response length." It shows the whole trade-off in one picture. Alternative: Figure 1 (p.1) for sequential vs parallel vs async structure, or Figure 2 (p.3) for the Fork/Join protocol.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure and table text extracted somewhat garbled (Table 2 columns run together, e.g. "38.72048.0"; I separated them by hand: 38.7 and 2048.0). Fig 5 bar values were read from flattened text, so the baseline-to-method mapping is from the paper's prose. Table 3 header is labelled "−RU Reward" in the text but "−Rη Reward" in the table; the same thing. The extracted text had no explicit Appendix word beyond the titles; the appendix figures (9-11) are case studies only, no extra numbers. Extraction saved at /tmp/asy.txt.
